title: Why Light Never Speeds Up
question: Why can't you make light look faster by chasing it or running from it?
hook: Racing toward a beam of light gets you no closer to catching it.
idea: Light has the same speed for every observer, so time itself must run differently for objects in motion.

beats.prompt: A train races past a station, faster and faster each run. Each time, observers measure the speed of a light signal sent from the station to the train. What happens to the measured speed?

choices.label: It stays exactly the same however fast the train goes
It grows with the train's speed
choices.feedback: This is the everyday habit of adding speeds, but light does not follow it.

choices.label: It shrinks as the train speeds up
choices.feedback: Moving does not slow the light down either; its speed does not depend on the train.

beats.explain: The second postulate says light travels at the same speed for everyone, so the signal keeps one speed no matter how fast the train goes.

beats.prompt: match each idea to what it says
pairs: Physics laws are identical in all inertial frames
Light has one speed for all observers
Replaces the Galilean one between moving frames
beats.explain: Two postulates plus the tools that follow from them: a new way to compare frames and a quantity every observer agrees on.

items: Elapsed time between two events on a clock
Laws of physics in inertial frames
beats.explain: Time on clocks depends on motion, while light speed, the interval and the laws of physics are shared by all inertial observers.

beats.prompt: put these steps toward special relativity in order
items: Galileo describes the principle of relativity with a ship
Maxwell's electromagnetism predicts a constant light speed
The Michelson–Morley experiment confirms a constant light speed
Relativity is extended to include gravity in general relativity
beats.explain: Galileo came in 1632, Maxwell in 1864, Michelson–Morley in 1887 and general relativity in 1916.
